questions.question: A patient with repaired TOF and a native patched RVOT is being assessed for transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement. CMR has quantified pulmonary regurgitation and RV volumes. Which additional examination is recommended by the 2025 ACHD guideline to determine anatomical suitability?
options: TEE confined to pulmonary valve leaflet motion
Repeat cine CMR confined to RV end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes
Cardiac CT defining RVOT geometry and coronary relationships
A right-heart saturation run without anatomical imaging
questions.explanation:
Cardiac CT Before Native-RVOT Transcatheter Pulmonary Valve Treatment

Correct answer: Cardiac CT defining RVOT geometry and coronary relationships

Procedure-Specific Anatomy

**The 2025 guideline recommends cardiac CT for repaired TOF with native RVOT anatomy when transcatheter pulmonary valve treatment is being considered.** The purpose is anatomical suitability, not replacement of the preceding CMR functional assessment.

Define the intended landing zone, its dimensions and shape, pulmonary artery anatomy and the coronary course relative to the outflow tract. A favorable regurgitant fraction or RV volume does not by itself establish that a device can be implanted safely.

CT planning and device selection are anatomy specific. A native patched RVOT and an RV-to-PA conduit do not have identical dimensions, mechanical constraints or procedural approaches.

Coronary Compression and Alternative Repair

**Expansion within the RVOT can compress a neighboring coronary artery.** The consequence can be acute ischemia, so coronary proximity is a central safety issue rather than an incidental imaging finding.

Selected balloon-expandable conduit or RVOT procedures use test balloon inflation with simultaneous coronary angiography to assess compression. Apply the appropriate device-specific pathway; neither a generic negative test nor a simple coronary-distance estimate guarantees safety for every device.

Demonstrated compression risk or unsuitable landing anatomy can favor surgical or another tailored approach. Assess associated lesions that may also need repair, and discuss valve durability, endocarditis, residual obstruction/regurgitation and follow-up. The examination is chosen because it answers a specific procedural anatomy question that a repeated RV-volume study or oximetry run does not.

TEE confined to pulmonary valve leaflet motion: TEE can answer selected valve questions but does not replace the recommended cross-sectional definition of the large patched RVOT, landing-zone geometry and neighboring coronary arteries.

Repeat cine CMR confined to RV end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes: Those measurements are central to ventricular assessment and have already been obtained. Repeating only volumetry does not provide the additional detailed RVOT/device-planning assessment requested here.

A right-heart saturation run without anatomical imaging: Invasive sampling can characterize shunting and pressure-flow physiology when indicated. It does not define the dimensions, shape and coronary proximity needed to determine suitability of a native RVOT for a particular transcatheter valve.

questions.question: An adult with repaired TOF has worsening exercise tolerance. CMR pulmonary regurgitant fraction is 12%, but imaging shows substantial RVOT obstruction. RV systolic pressure is 90 mmHg while systemic systolic pressure is 120 mmHg; distal PA pressure is not elevated. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Wait until RV end-systolic volume exceeds the regurgitation-related referral marker
Defer intervention assessment until pulmonary regurgitant fraction reaches 25%
Treat presumed PAH solely because RV systolic pressure is 90 mmHg
Refer for assessment of relief of the residual RVOT obstruction
questions.explanation:
Pressure-Loaded RV After TOF Repair

Correct answer: Refer for assessment of relief of the residual RVOT obstruction

Pressure Versus Volume Loading

**Residual RVOT obstruction can create important pulmonary valve/outflow dysfunction despite little regurgitation.** Here RV pressure is 90/120 = 0.75 of systemic, exceeding two-thirds systemic pressure.

Distinguish valvar, subvalvar, conduit and branch pulmonary arterial obstruction. Define where the pressure drop occurs and whether another lesion contributes to exercise limitation.

A high RV pressure is not automatically pulmonary hypertension: obstruction between the RV and PA can generate the difference. Interpret tricuspid-regurgitation-derived RV pressure estimates within the known outflow anatomy.

Intervention Assessment and Follow-Up

**Symptoms with important residual obstruction warrant specialist repair assessment rather than waiting for severe regurgitation or advanced ventricular dilation.** The procedure depends on the actual level and anatomy of the lesion.

Options may include catheter relief or valve intervention for a suitable target, while complex muscular, patched or associated lesions may favor surgery. CMR, CT, Doppler and selected catheter measurements answer complementary functional and anatomical questions.

Review RV and LV function, tricuspid regurgitation, arrhythmias and objective exercise measurements. A fall in exercise capacity can result from multiple residual lesions, so intervention planning should not use a single number in isolation. After treatment, follow residual gradients, new or persisting regurgitation and ventricular response. Relief of the mechanical load does not remove the established scar-related arrhythmia substrate.

Wait until RV end-systolic volume exceeds the regurgitation-related referral marker: Volume criteria are important in selected regurgitant repaired-TOF pathways. Waiting for that marker alone can overlook symptomatic pressure-overload disease and inappropriate application of one phenotype’s thresholds to another.

Defer intervention assessment until pulmonary regurgitant fraction reaches 25%: A regurgitant threshold addresses one form of pulmonary valve dysfunction. Significant obstructive pressure loading is another; the low regurgitant fraction does not negate the symptomatic RVOT problem.

Treat presumed PAH solely because RV systolic pressure is 90 mmHg: RV systolic pressure approximates PA systolic pressure only in the absence of important intervening obstruction. The supplied RVOT lesion and lower distal PA pressure localize the pressure load rather than establishing PAH.

questions.question: A 34-year-old with a large unrepaired VSD had pulmonary overcirculation in childhood. Current catheterization shows mean PA pressure 75 mmHg, wedge pressure 10 mmHg, PVR 18 Wood units and Qp/Qs 0.8. Systemic saturation is 82%, with bidirectional flow and no RV outflow obstruction. Which PAH-CHD category best fits?
options: PAH associated with a small coincidental defect
Eisenmenger syndrome
PAH persisting after correction of a congenital defect
PAH with a prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt
questions.explanation:
Eisenmenger Syndrome Within PAH Associated With Congenital Shunts

Correct answer: Eisenmenger syndrome

Evolution of the Pulmonary Vascular Lesion

**A large congenital systemic-to-pulmonary communication can produce progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling.** As resistance rises, the original flow excess diminishes and eventually becomes bidirectional or predominantly right-to-left.

The low wedge pressure supports a precapillary process rather than isolated pulmonary venous hypertension. The history establishes the causal large shunt; cyanosis alone would not distinguish pulmonary vascular disease from restricted pulmonary flow in another congenital lesion.

Implications for Repair and Ongoing Care

**Established Eisenmenger physiology is not an uncomplicated closure indication.** Eliminating the communication can remove a pressure-relief route and precipitate severe right-heart failure.

A fall in pulmonary pressure during treatment does not by itself establish reversibility or justify closure. Expert assessment integrates resistance, flow direction, filling pressures and ventricular function; selected treat-and-repair pathways for other shunt phenotypes must not be transferred automatically.

Management includes ACHD and pulmonary-hypertension expertise, functional assessment, iron and renal monitoring, and evaluation for targeted PAH therapy. Bleeding, arrhythmia, paradoxical embolism and infection can complicate cyanotic disease. Pregnancy counseling is essential because maternal risk is very high. Intravascular procedures require meticulous exclusion of air from lines when right-to-left passage is possible.

PAH-CHD group | Distinguishing context

Eisenmenger | Large causal shunt with advanced pulmonary vascular disease and reversal

Prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt | Predominantly left-to-right flow remains

Small/coincidental defect | Defect insufficient to explain the pulmonary vascular disease

After correction | PAH persists or develops after anatomical repair

PAH associated with a small coincidental defect: Small defects can coexist with a pulmonary arteriopathy resembling idiopathic PAH, without having caused the vascular disease. This patient instead has a large longstanding shunt, documented earlier overcirculation and subsequent reversal of its net direction.

PAH persisting after correction of a congenital defect: PAH may persist or emerge after surgical or catheter correction. That category requires a repaired defect; the supplied VSD remains open and is the route for desaturated systemic flow.

PAH with a prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt: That group retains predominant left-to-right flow, generally without resting cyanosis from shunt reversal. The current net Qp/Qs below one and arterial desaturation place this patient in the Eisenmenger group.

questions.question: A stable adult with Eisenmenger syndrome has hemoglobin 22 g/dL, hematocrit 68%, MCV 88 fL and ferritin 70 micrograms/L. Hydration is adequate, and there is no headache, visual disturbance or other hyperviscosity symptom. Which approach to the erythrocytosis is best?
options: Start aspirin solely to counter the elevated red-cell mass
Perform isovolumic phlebotomy because hematocrit exceeds 65%
Schedule repeated phlebotomy to achieve the hematocrit target used in polycythemia vera
Maintain hydration and monitor without scheduled phlebotomy
questions.explanation:
Compensated Secondary Erythrocytosis in Cyanotic CHD

Correct answer: Maintain hydration and monitor without scheduled phlebotomy

Oxygen Transport and Compensatory Red-Cell Mass

**Chronic arterial desaturation stimulates erythropoiesis.** An increased hemoglobin concentration helps preserve oxygen content when the saturation of each hemoglobin molecule is reduced.

The hemoglobin value therefore requires interpretation with oxygen saturation, symptoms and iron status. A high value in this setting does not by itself establish a myeloproliferative neoplasm or a need to normalize the count.

When Symptoms Change the Assessment

**Persistent hyperviscosity is a clinical diagnosis after competing causes are considered.** Review hydration and iron indices before attributing fatigue, headache or dizziness to the hematocrit.

The current ACHD pathway considers phlebotomy for persistent symptoms with hematocrit above ==65%== despite adequate hydration and iron repletion. If selected, it requires experienced supervision with isovolumic replacement, not repeated unsupervised blood donation.

New severe headache, fever, focal neurological findings or altered consciousness requires urgent evaluation for causes such as stroke or brain abscess. It should not be labeled hyperviscosity from a blood count alone. Follow-up includes symptoms, saturation, full blood count and iron indices. Inappropriate repeated venesection can create iron deficiency even while the absolute hemoglobin remains above the usual laboratory reference interval.

Start aspirin solely to counter the elevated red-cell mass: Antiplatelet therapy has established indications in atherosclerotic disease and selected hematological settings. Cyanotic erythrocytosis alone does not establish benefit, while abnormal hemostasis can increase bleeding risk.

Perform isovolumic phlebotomy because hematocrit exceeds 65%: Expert isovolumic phlebotomy may be considered for persistent clinically important hyperviscosity after dehydration and iron deficiency are corrected. Exceeding a numerical threshold without symptoms does not supply that indication.

Schedule repeated phlebotomy to achieve the hematocrit target used in polycythemia vera: Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative disorder with a different thrombotic mechanism and treatment target. Applying its target to adaptive hypoxemic erythrocytosis can impair oxygen delivery and deplete iron.

questions.question: A cyanotic adult has increasing fatigue, hemoglobin 19 g/dL, hematocrit 60%, MCV 66 fL, ferritin 7 micrograms/L and transferrin saturation 8%. There is no acute bleeding or hemodynamic deterioration. Which strategy best addresses the laboratory abnormality?
options: Replace iron with monitored reassessment of blood count and iron indices
Withhold iron because the hemoglobin is already above the laboratory reference range
Perform venesection before giving iron to prevent a further hematocrit increase
Defer iron until a hemoglobinopathy panel explains the microcytosis
questions.explanation:
Iron Deficiency Despite an Elevated Hemoglobin

Correct answer: Replace iron with monitored reassessment of blood count and iron indices

Recognizing Relative Hematological Inadequacy

**Laboratory reference ranges derived from noncyanotic adults can conceal iron deficiency in cyanotic CHD.** Interpret hemoglobin alongside saturation and iron studies rather than using a high hemoglobin to exclude deficiency.

Microcytosis supports the finding but is not a substitute for ferritin and transferrin saturation. Inflammatory states can complicate ferritin interpretation; the very low ferritin in this case is persuasive evidence of depleted stores.

Replacement, Evidence and Monitoring

**Correct the deficiency and investigate its source.** Review dietary intake, menstrual or gastrointestinal loss and prior phlebotomy. Route and dose depend on tolerability, severity and the specialist treatment plan.

A small prospective cyanotic-CHD study used oral ferrous fumarate titrated up to ==200 mg== three times daily for three months. This is the mass of the iron salt, not ==200 mg== of elemental iron per dose, and is a study protocol rather than a mandatory starting regimen.

That study found improved iron stores, walking performance and reported quality of life; peak oxygen uptake did not significantly improve. Its uncontrolled design and mixed congenital population limit causal and survival claims. Recheck clinical response, hemoglobin and iron indices, and adjust replacement rather than withholding needed iron merely because erythropoiesis may increase. Persistent symptoms after correction require assessment for cardiac, pulmonary vascular and other systemic causes.

Withhold iron because the hemoglobin is already above the laboratory reference range: A raised hemoglobin can be an appropriate response to hypoxemia. It does not exclude depleted stores; low ferritin and transferrin saturation provide direct evidence of iron deficiency here.

Perform venesection before giving iron to prevent a further hematocrit increase: Venesection may have a narrow role in persistent symptomatic hyperviscosity after other factors are corrected. In this iron-deficient patient it would remove additional iron and red cells rather than address the demonstrated deficiency.

Defer iron until a hemoglobinopathy panel explains the microcytosis: Thalassemia is a genuine cause of microcytosis and may coexist. However, the depleted iron indices already justify replacement and assessment of its cause; persistent unexplained microcytosis can subsequently prompt additional testing.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes randomized endothelin-receptor-antagonist evidence in Eisenmenger syndrome?
options: BREATHE-5 established bosentan superiority over sildenafil in a direct randomized comparison
MAESTRO met its primary endpoint by improving six-minute walk distance over placebo
BREATHE-5 improved pulmonary vascular resistance without worsening systemic oxygen saturation
MAESTRO demonstrated lower mortality as its primary treatment effect
questions.explanation:
Interpreting Eisenmenger Endothelin-Antagonist Trials

Correct answer: BREATHE-5 improved pulmonary vascular resistance without worsening systemic oxygen saturation

Population and Endpoint Matter

**BREATHE-5 enrolled 54 WHO functional class III patients and compared bosentan with placebo for 16 weeks.** Oxygen saturation was the primary safety endpoint and pulmonary vascular resistance the primary efficacy endpoint.

The trial also found a favorable walking-distance effect. It supported treatment without the feared deterioration in systemic oxygenation; it was not a head-to-head trial or a mortality trial.

MAESTRO enrolled 226 patients, included a more heterogeneous population and permitted selected background PAH treatment. Its negative primary exercise endpoint must remain explicit despite exploratory findings. Different populations and trial conduct prevent a simple indirect ranking of the two agents.

Applying Treatment and Monitoring

**Bosentan blocks both ETA and ETB receptors.** For an adult weighing more than 40 kg, the labeled oral regimen starts at ==62.5 mg== twice daily and increases after four weeks to ==125 mg== twice daily if appropriate.

Obtain aminotransferases before treatment and monthly thereafter; monitor hemoglobin, fluid retention and interactions. Pregnancy is contraindicated. Effective contraception is required during treatment and for one month after stopping, and bosentan can reduce hormonal contraceptive effectiveness.

Therapy is selected and escalated by congenital and PAH specialists according to symptoms, functional assessment and response. ERA and PDE5-inhibitor strategies should not be judged from a false claim that every ERA trial was positive. Persistent deterioration warrants reassessment of the full physiology and specialist escalation rather than simply reproducing a regimen from an unrelated PAH population.

Trial | Treatment / primary outcome interpretation

BREATHE-5, 16 weeks | Bosentan: PVR benefit; systemic saturation safety preserved

MAESTRO, 16 weeks | Macitentan: primary 6-minute walk superiority not demonstrated

BREATHE-5 established bosentan superiority over sildenafil in a direct randomized comparison: BREATHE-5 compared bosentan with placebo. It did not randomize patients between an endothelin antagonist and a PDE5 inhibitor, so it cannot establish comparative superiority between those drug classes.

MAESTRO met its primary endpoint by improving six-minute walk distance over placebo: MAESTRO studied macitentan in a broader Eisenmenger population, but did not show superiority for the primary six-minute walk endpoint. Exploratory biomarker and hemodynamic signals cannot be relabeled as a positive primary endpoint.

MAESTRO demonstrated lower mortality as its primary treatment effect: MAESTRO assessed exercise capacity over 16 weeks, not a primary mortality endpoint. A short-term functional trial does not establish a survival benefit simply because its drug is used in PAH.

questions.question: An adult with Eisenmenger syndrome is in sinus rhythm, has no prior venous thromboembolism, no intracardiac thrombus and no mechanical valve. There have been intermittent minor hemoptysis episodes. Which long-term antithrombotic strategy is most appropriate solely for the Eisenmenger diagnosis?
options: Start a vitamin K antagonist to prevent pulmonary vascular thrombosis
Do not prescribe routine oral anticoagulation; reassess if a separate indication develops
Start a direct oral anticoagulant because it avoids INR monitoring
Use aspirin as a lower-intensity substitute for preventive anticoagulation
questions.explanation:
Antithrombotic Decisions in Eisenmenger Syndrome

Correct answer: Do not prescribe routine oral anticoagulation; reassess if a separate indication develops

Simultaneous Thrombotic and Hemorrhagic Risk

**Cyanotic CHD can produce both thrombosis and bleeding.** Altered platelet number or function and coagulation abnormalities coexist with vascular dilation, stasis and possible thrombus formation.

An elevated hematocrit does not mean that all clinical risk is thrombotic or that antithrombotic treatment will improve outcomes. The presence, location and likely age of any detected thrombus matter; organized in-situ pulmonary arterial thrombus is not automatically equivalent to a new embolic event.

Separate Indications and Bleeding Assessment

**Current ACHD guidance advises against routine oral anticoagulation for Eisenmenger syndrome alone.** Reconsider treatment if atrial arrhythmia, documented thromboembolism, a mechanical prosthesis or another independent indication appears.

Even with an indication, review bleeding history, platelet count, renal and hepatic function, concurrent drugs and the proposed agent with experienced clinicians. A mechanical valve has a specific vitamin K antagonist requirement; one should not substitute a DOAC merely to simplify follow-up.

Active significant hemoptysis requires urgent clinical assessment and stabilization, with investigation of its cause and specialist decisions about antithrombotic interruption or reversal when relevant. Recurrent minor bleeding also deserves evaluation. If warfarin is used, a markedly high hematocrit requires the laboratory to consider citrate adjustment for coagulation sampling, because standard sampling can distort results. The decision is driven by the actual competing risks rather than a universal procoagulant label.

Start a vitamin K antagonist to prevent pulmonary vascular thrombosis: A vitamin K antagonist may be appropriate for a separate established indication after individualized assessment. Eisenmenger physiology alone has not shown a preventive survival benefit sufficient to offset its bleeding risk.

Start a direct oral anticoagulant because it avoids INR monitoring: Convenience does not create an anticoagulation indication. A DOAC requires an appropriate thromboembolic indication, consideration of the congenital phenotype, renal function and bleeding risk; none is established by the supplied history alone.

Use aspirin as a lower-intensity substitute for preventive anticoagulation: Aspirin has distinct arterial indications but is not a proven substitute for routine thromboprophylaxis in cyanotic CHD. It can also worsen bleeding, including in a patient with hemoptysis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old with severe tricuspid regurgitation has a septal tricuspid leaflet hinge point 18 mm apical to the anterior mitral leaflet insertion in the four-chamber view. Body surface area is 1.8 m². Which structural diagnosis is best supported?

Ventricular functional tricuspid regurgitation
questions.explanation:

Correct answer: Ebstein anomaly

questions.question: An adult with Ebstein anomaly is being assessed for tricuspid valve surgery. The ECG shows ventricular pre-excitation, although the patient reports no sustained palpitation. Which additional step is best supported before the operation?
options: Begin an AV-nodal blocking drug as definitive management of the pre-excitation
Ambulatory monitoring alone, reserving pathway assessment for documented sustained tachycardia
Proceed with valve repair and defer pathway assessment until after surgery
Expert electrophysiological study to assess accessory pathways and potential ablation
questions.explanation:
Accessory-Pathway Assessment Before Tricuspid Repair

Correct answer: Expert electrophysiological study to assess accessory pathways and potential ablation

Risk Beyond Symptom Frequency

**Ebstein anomaly is associated with accessory atrioventricular pathways, sometimes multiple.** A patient can have clinically important antegrade conduction without a reliable history of sustained palpitations.

The pathway can support AV reentrant tachycardia. During atrial fibrillation, rapid antegrade conduction over a high-risk pathway can produce dangerous ventricular rates. A resting tracing identifies pre-excitation but does not provide the complete risk assessment.

Sequence Assessment With Valve Treatment

**The 2025 ACHD guideline recommends EP study for symptomatic arrhythmia or asymptomatic ventricular pre-excitation in Ebstein anomaly.** The aim is to identify substrates suitable for ablation, including multiple or high-risk pathways.

High-risk accessory conduction or multiple pathways supports ablation. Before tricuspid surgery, an expert EP approach is useful because repair can make later access to pathways and other arrhythmia substrates more difficult. The precise ablation plan is based on mapping and conduction properties, not on an assumption that every delta wave has identical risk.

Acute management still depends on rhythm and stability. Hemodynamic instability warrants synchronized cardioversion; irregular pre-excited tachycardia should not be treated with isolated AV-nodal blockade. Long-term successful pathway ablation does not correct severe tricuspid regurgitation, so structural and electrical treatment remain coordinated parts of the same care plan.

Begin an AV-nodal blocking drug as definitive management of the pre-excitation: AV-nodal blockers treat selected regular supraventricular rhythms but do not eliminate an accessory pathway. They can be hazardous in pre-excited AF, where conduction over the pathway may accelerate ventricular activation.

Ambulatory monitoring alone, reserving pathway assessment for documented sustained tachycardia: Ambulatory monitoring can document intermittent arrhythmia but does not reliably define antegrade accessory-pathway risk or exclude multiple pathways. Current guidance supports EP assessment for asymptomatic pre-excitation in Ebstein anomaly.

Proceed with valve repair and defer pathway assessment until after surgery: Valve surgery may alter or impede catheter access to relevant right-sided substrates. The absence of reported sustained tachycardia does not remove the rationale for assessing manifest pre-excitation before repair.

questions.question: A 38-year-old underwent a Senning operation for d-TGA. Resting saturation is 96%, falling reproducibly to 84% on exercise. Systemic RV function is unchanged, with no important new valve regurgitation or pulmonary disease. Which residual lesion should be specifically sought?
options: A baffle leak allowing systemic venous blood to reach the systemic arterial circuit
Isolated systemic venous baffle stenosis without a leak
Isolated systemic tricuspid regurgitation without a shunt
Isolated chronotropic incompetence from sinus-node dysfunction
questions.explanation:
Exertional Desaturation After an Atrial Switch

Correct answer: A baffle leak allowing systemic venous blood to reach the systemic arterial circuit

Follow the Surgically Redirected Blood

**Mustard and Senning procedures redirect venous return within the atria.** The morphological RV still pumps to the aorta, and the morphological LV remains subpulmonary.

The systemic venous baffle normally channels caval blood toward the mitral valve and LV. A leak can permit desaturated systemic venous blood to enter the pulmonary venous atrium, then the systemic RV and aorta. Pressure relationships during exercise can make desaturation more evident than at rest.

Imaging and Intervention Assessment

**Define both baffle integrity and patency.** Contrast echocardiography, CMR and selected transesophageal or catheter assessment answer complementary questions about communication, obstruction and flow.

An arm injection can miss an inferior systemic venous baffle leak; injection site should match the anatomy being interrogated. CMR also assesses systemic RV volumes, function and associated lesions. A negative limited study should not be treated as proof that every baffle segment is normal.

A symptomatic leak requires congenital specialist assessment for closure when appropriate, with evaluation of the hemodynamic consequences. Before transvenous device leads, assess leaks and obstruction because systemic embolic risk and venous access issues may alter the procedure. Lifelong review also looks for systemic RV failure, systemic tricuspid regurgitation, atrial tachyarrhythmia and sinus-node disease.

Isolated systemic venous baffle stenosis without a leak: Baffle stenosis can restrict preload, cause venous congestion and reduce exercise output. Without a communication or another source of admixture, obstruction alone does not directly explain systemic arterial desaturation.

Isolated systemic tricuspid regurgitation without a shunt: Systemic AV-valve regurgitation contributes to systemic RV failure and exercise intolerance. It does not directly mix desaturated venous blood into the arterial circuit, and no important new regurgitation is present here.

Isolated chronotropic incompetence from sinus-node dysfunction: Sinus-node dysfunction is common after atrial switch and can limit cardiac output during exercise. It usually produces an inadequate heart-rate response rather than a reproducible arterial oxygen-saturation fall of this magnitude.

questions.question: A stable 29-year-old who had an arterial switch for d-TGA develops exertional chest pressure with new regional LV dysfunction. TTE shows no major neoaortic valve lesion. Renal function is normal. Which targeted investigation most directly defines a surgically related coronary anatomical cause?
options: Exercise stress echocardiography focused on inducible wall-motion abnormalities
Vasodilator stress CMR focused on myocardial perfusion
Coronary CT angiography focused on the reimplanted coronary origins and proximal course
Exercise ECG focused on reproducible ST-segment changes
questions.explanation:
Coronary Assessment After an Arterial Switch

Correct answer: Coronary CT angiography focused on the reimplanted coronary origins and proximal course

Repair Determines the Late Complication

**An arterial switch moves the great arteries and transfers the coronary arteries to the neoaorta.** The LV becomes the systemic ventricle, unlike the systemic RV after an atrial switch.

Late coronary ostial narrowing, kinking or another proximal abnormality can cause ischemia. New symptoms, ventricular dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmia should prompt focused evaluation rather than reassurance based on young age and a low atherosclerotic risk profile.

Anatomical and Functional Evaluation

**Current ACHD guidance supports coronary evaluation when symptoms suggest ischemia after arterial switch.** CT usually provides the initial focused anatomical assessment; dedicated CMR or invasive angiography can be appropriate depending on the question and patient.

Anatomical imaging defines the origins, proximal course and relation to the reconstructed great vessels. Functional perfusion assessment or catheter investigation may still be needed if symptoms persist despite unrevealing cross-sectional findings, because dynamic obstruction or functional significance can remain uncertain.

The stable vignette asks for a targeted anatomical test. An acute coronary syndrome or unstable presentation instead requires urgent clinical management. Ongoing surveillance also includes the neoaortic root and valve, neopulmonary outflow and branch pulmonary arteries. The Lecompte-related arterial relationships and coronary transfer make this a different follow-up problem from atrial baffle obstruction or leak.

Exercise stress echocardiography focused on inducible wall-motion abnormalities: Stress echocardiography can identify a functional ischemic response. It does not usually define the transferred coronary origins and their proximal anatomical relation to reconstructed great vessels.

Vasodilator stress CMR focused on myocardial perfusion: Stress CMR can assess inducible ischemia and may be needed to determine functional significance. A perfusion-focused study does not directly map the reimplanted ostia and proximal course as requested; a dedicated coronary CMR protocol is a different investigation.

Exercise ECG focused on reproducible ST-segment changes: Exercise ECG can relate symptoms to exertion and identify an ischemic electrical response. It does not show ostial narrowing or the proximal surgical coronary course, so it cannot directly resolve the anatomical question.

questions.question: An unoperated adult has AV discordance and ventriculoarterial discordance. The left-sided ventricle has coarse trabeculations and a moderator band, and ejects into the aorta. New complete AV block accompanies worsening systemic AV-valve regurgitation. Which valve and ventricle form the systemic pump?
options: Morphological tricuspid valve and morphological left ventricle
Morphological mitral valve and morphological left ventricle
Morphological tricuspid valve and morphological right ventricle
Morphological mitral valve and morphological right ventricle
questions.explanation:
Systemic AV-Valve Disease in Congenitally Corrected TGA

Correct answer: Morphological tricuspid valve and morphological right ventricle

Two Discordances Restore the Sequence

**In ccTGA, AV and ventriculoarterial discordance occur together.** Systemic venous blood reaches the pulmonary artery through the morphological LV, while pulmonary venous blood reaches the aorta through the morphological RV.

The circulation is therefore physiologically in series, even though its connections are abnormal. Use segmental anatomy and ventricular markers; a left-sided chamber is not necessarily an LV. Associated VSD, pulmonary obstruction and an Ebstein-like systemic tricuspid valve can modify presentation.

Conduction, Valve and Ventricular Surveillance

**The systemic RV and its tricuspid valve face chronic systemic loading.** Regurgitation and ventricular dysfunction can reinforce each other, making serial valve and ventricular assessment essential.

Abnormal conduction-system anatomy predisposes to AV block, which can develop without surgery. Symptomatic complete block requires urgent rhythm assessment and pacing planning. Pacing route, ventricular activation and the risk of dyssynchrony require congenital EP expertise; a routine device approach may not suit the anatomy.

Valve intervention decisions should be made before advanced irreversible systemic RV dysfunction when possible, with expert evaluation of symptoms, regurgitation and ventricular response. Do not assume that evidence and thresholds for an ordinary systemic LV transfer unchanged. Follow-up also evaluates associated defects, arrhythmias and exercise capacity; the word corrected describes the circulatory sequence, not anatomical normality or freedom from lifelong complications.

Morphological tricuspid valve and morphological left ventricle: Identify the ventricle by its morphology rather than left-right position. The moderator band and coarse trabeculation support an RV, and the AV valve connected to it is morphologically tricuspid.

Morphological mitral valve and morphological left ventricle: That is the usual systemic pump and the expected arrangement after a successful arterial switch with AV concordance. Here double discordance routes pulmonary venous blood through a morphological RV to the aorta.

Morphological mitral valve and morphological right ventricle: An AV valve is named by its morphological ventricular connection, not merely by which side of the chest it occupies. In the supplied concordance pattern of valve-to-ventricular morphology, the systemic RV has a tricuspid inlet.

  • B — Morphological mitral valve and morphological left ventricle: That is the usual systemic pump and the expected arrangement after a successful arterial switch with AV concordance. Here double discordance routes pulmonary venous blood through a morphological RV to the aorta.
  • D — Morphological mitral valve and morphological right ventricle: An AV valve is named by its morphological ventricular connection, not merely by which side of the chest it occupies. In the supplied concordance pattern of valve-to-ventricular morphology, the systemic RV has a tricuspid inlet.

bullets.text: **In ccTGA, AV and ventriculoarterial discordance occur together.** Systemic venous blood reaches the pulmonary artery through the morphological LV, while pulmonary venous blood reaches the aorta through the morphological RV.
children: The circulation is therefore physiologically in series, even though its connections are abnormal. Use segmental anatomy and ventricular markers; a left-sided chamber is not necessarily an LV. Associated VSD, pulmonary obstruction and an Ebstein-like systemic tricuspid valve can modify presentation.

bullets.text: **The systemic RV and its tricuspid valve face chronic systemic loading.** Regurgitation and ventricular dysfunction can reinforce each other, making serial valve and ventricular assessment essential.
children: Abnormal conduction-system anatomy predisposes to AV block, which can develop without surgery. Symptomatic complete block requires urgent rhythm assessment and pacing planning. Pacing route, ventricular activation and the risk of dyssynchrony require congenital EP expertise; a routine device approach may not suit the anatomy.

Valve intervention decisions should be made before advanced irreversible systemic RV dysfunction when possible, with expert evaluation of symptoms, regurgitation and ventricular response. Do not assume that evidence and thresholds for an ordinary systemic LV transfer unchanged. Follow-up also evaluates associated defects, arrhythmias and exercise capacity; the word corrected describes the circulatory sequence, not anatomical normality or freedom from lifelong complications.
